title: This founder is teaching chips how to recycle (their energy)
gist: Vaire Computing cofounder Hannah Earley built a patent-pending resonator chip component that proved reversible computing can recover more energy than it consumes, a decades-old theoretical concept now validated in hardware for the first time, though experts caution it remains early-stage for data-center commercialization.

insights.claim: Reversible computing treats the heat dissipated by conventional chips as an avoidable design choice rather than an inevitable cost: conventional chips erase intermediate information during a calculation and dissipate energy as heat in the process, whereas a reversible circuit retains that information so the computation can be run backward, recovering some of the energy.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Reframes chip energy efficiency as a fundamentally different circuit-design paradigm rather than incremental process-node shrinkage, a potential structural alternative to Moore's Law-style scaling for cutting data center power use.
insights.locator: When conventional computer chips perform calculations

insights.claim: Earley compares conventional computing to racing through a city and pumping the brakes at every intersection, losing momentum and burning more fuel to accelerate again, whereas reversible computing aims to keep the computational 'momentum' going and recover energy instead of losing it.
insights.speaker: Hannah Earley, via Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: A clear mental model for why reversible computing could meaningfully cut energy use in high-throughput compute environments like data centers, laptops, and phones.
insights.locator: Earley compares the approach to racing through a city

insights.claim: The concept of reversible computing was first proposed more than 50 years ago but proved impractical to implement with existing transistors and circuit designs until now.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Establishes that Vaire is attempting to commercialize a long-theorized but never-realized computing paradigm, raising both the scientific stakes and the execution risk.
insights.locator: While the idea was first proposed more than 50 years ago

insights.claim: Earley designed a patent-pending resonator, a microscopic chip component that stores recovered energy for later reuse, and last year Vaire Computing announced a chip using this resonator recovered more energy than it lost, even after accounting for the energy needed to power the resonator itself.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: The first net-positive energy-recovery demonstration for a subfield that had existed mostly in theory, a milestone that could de-risk future funding and partnership discussions for Vaire.
insights.locator: Last year, Vaire announced a key breakthrough

insights.claim: An electronic design automation researcher and former University of Michigan professor calls the result 'interesting' but says the technology is still quite early stage and Vaire will need a series of increasingly realistic and convincing demonstrations to attract the industry support needed for commercialization.
insights.speaker: Igor Markov, via Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: An independent expert's tempered view sets realistic expectations for Vaire's commercialization timeline, useful for gauging how far the technology is from data-center deployment.
insights.quote: a series of increasingly realistic and convincing demonstrations to attract the industry support needed for commercialization
insights.locator: It's clear they have something interesting

insights.claim: Vaire Computing, cofounded by Hannah Earley in 2021, has raised more than $12 million and hired Michael Frank — author of the seminal 1999 PhD thesis on reversible computing — as a senior scientist.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Quantifies Vaire's funding scale and shows it has recruited the field's original theoretical pioneer, a credibility and talent-depth signal for an early-stage deep-tech bet.
insights.locator: The pair cofounded Vaire that same year

insights.claim: Earley believes the future of chip design lies not in further refining existing chip architectures but in rebuilding computer chips from the ground up with reversibility as the organizing principle, aiming to make data centers, laptops, and phones much more energy efficient.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Signals Vaire's ambition extends beyond a niche component to a full architectural rethink, implying a longer development timeline but potentially much larger addressable impact if realized across data centers and consumer devices.
insights.quote: I want to tackle every part of how computers are built, and rethink it in these terms.
insights.locator: Earley and her colleagues' next challenge

insights.claim: Earley's PhD advisor, computational biologist Gos Micklem, sent her Michael Frank's 1999 PhD thesis on reversible computing while she was originally studying DNA-based computation; after initial skepticism and weeks of reflection, she became convinced the connection between information, energy, and heat could change computers forever, which redirected her entire PhD toward reversible computing theory and software.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Traces the intellectual lineage from Frank's original 1999 theory directly to Vaire's current commercial hardware effort, underscoring how long the idea incubated before finding a viable implementation path.
insights.locator: a few months in, Micklem sent her the 1999 PhD thesis
